questions.prompt: Why can't an attacker avoid Event ID 1102 by clearing the log repeatedly?
options: 1102 is stored on a separate partition
Each clear writes a new 1102 immediately afterward, so the newly-empty log always contains a record of the clearing
Clearing twice restores the original log
questions.explanation: Suppressing it requires stopping the Event Log service or tampering below it, which produces its own detectable gaps rather than silence.

questions.prompt: Why are individual event records often recoverable after a log is cleared?
options: Windows keeps an automatic backup of every log
Clearing does not overwrite the disk sectors, and EVTX records have recognizable structure that allows carving from unallocated space
The records are duplicated in the registry
Cleared logs are moved to the Recycle Bin
questions.explanation: EVTX chunks and records carry identifiable signatures, so tools like EVTXtract and bulk_extractor can recover individual records from unallocated space and slack.

questions.prompt: Why does Windows Event Forwarding turn log clearing against the attacker?
options: WEF prevents logs from being cleared at all
A copy already exists on the collector beyond the attacker's reach, so clearing destroys nothing while still generating 1102
WEF encrypts the local log files
questions.explanation: Forwarding converts an evidence-destruction technique into an evidence-creation one -- the attacker announces their presence without removing anything.

questions.prompt: Which category of surviving evidence is largest and most often overlooked?
options: Non-log artifacts -- MFT, USN journal, Prefetch, Amcache, ShimCache, registry timestamps, ShellBags, UserAssist -- all untouched by log clearing
questions.explanation: Clearing the Security log does nothing to the entire filesystem and registry artifact set, which frequently answers the question on its own.
